title: What is IAsyncEnumerable and when do you use await foreach?
description: Streaming async sequences: pulling rows lazily with EF Core, implementing your own async iterators, and cancellation.

data.text: **Question:** What is IAsyncEnumerable<T> and when do you use await foreach?

`IAsyncEnumerable<T>` is the async counterpart of `IEnumerable<T>`: a **lazy sequence where each item arrives asynchronously**. You consume it with `await foreach`, which awaits each `MoveNextAsync()` before yielding the next item. The canonical use case is streaming rows from a database (`AsAsyncEnumerable()` in EF Core) or paging an API **without materializing the whole result set** — memory stays bounded to one item, and backpressure follows the consumer's pace. Write your own with `async IAsyncEnumerable<T>` iterators, and always propagate `CancellationToken` via `[EnumeratorCancellation]`.

**Why it exists:**
- `ToListAsync()` on 10 million rows loads all 10 million — and you usually process one at a time
- Sync `IEnumerable` + `Task` per item doesn't compose: no standard protocol, easy to accidentally buffer
- IAsyncEnumerable gives the compiler a protocol (`GetAsyncEnumerator`, `MoveNextAsync`, `Current`) just like IEnumerable, but for `ValueTask<bool>` steps

**Consumption:**
- `await foreach (var row in query.AsAsyncEnumerable().WithCancellation(ct))` — one row in memory at a time
- `await foreach (var batch in EnumerateBatches(db, 500))` — bounded batches for bulk ops
- LINQ: async-aware operators live in `System.Linq.Async` (IAsyncEnumerable community/official package): `WhereAwait`, `SelectAwait`, `ToListAsync`, `FirstAwaitAsync`
- Don't call sync LINQ directly on the async sequence — enumerate first or use the async operators

**Writing an iterator:**
- `static async IAsyncEnumerable<T> Fetch([EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)` — the attribute wires `WithCancellation` to your token parameter
- `yield return` works the same as in sync iterators; every `yield` may await
- Exceptions surface at the await point of `MoveNextAsync` — the consumer's `await foreach` sees them

**Operational considerations:**
- **Streaming ≠ buffering**: if the consumer stops enumerating, the underlying command may still be open — dispose enumerators (`await foreach` disposes automatically)
- Long-lived readers hold a connection and an open DataReader for the whole enumeration — keep consumers fast or batch with keyset pagination instead for very long streams
- Cancellation: pass `[EnumeratorCancellation]` and honor it in your loops, or a hung consumer holds the connection forever
- When to prefer explicit batching (keyset pages of 1,000) over one giant async stream: bounded memory AND bounded transaction/connection time, resumability across process restarts
- Growable streams between services: IAsyncEnumerable is in-process — cross the wire with gRPC streaming, Channels, or message queues

data.caption: Pull-based flow: the consumer's await each MoveNextAsync drives one unit of work upstream — one item in memory at a time, natural backpressure.

Interviewers want to assess:
- The memory story: streaming vs materializing, and when each is right
- Correct cancellation propagation with [EnumeratorCancellation]
- Knowing the connection stays open for the whole enumeration
- Distinguishing in-process async streams from cross-service streaming

items: Enumerating a 5M-row stream slowly — the DataReader and connection stay open for the whole consumer lifetime
Forgetting [EnumeratorCancellation] — WithCancellation does nothing and shutdown hangs
Calling sync LINQ (Where/Select/Count) directly on IAsyncEnumerable — use System.Linq.Async operators
Buffering anyway: .ToListAsync() inside the first line of the loop defeats the purpose
Assuming early break cancels the database command — it stops pulling, but cancellation is what tears the command down promptly
Using IAsyncEnumerable across service boundaries — it's an in-process protocol; use gRPC streaming or queues over the wire

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: IAsyncEnumerable = lazy async sequence; await foreach pulls one item at a time
Canonical use: streaming DB rows or API pages without materializing
Streams hold a connection open — keep consumers fast or batch
Cross-process streaming needs gRPC/queues, not this interface
data.takeaway: Reach for await foreach when you process items one at a time and can't afford the full result set in memory — and always thread the cancellation token through.
